questions.stem: A physiology researcher is tracing the sequence of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis that ends in cortisol synthesis. Which of the following hormones is released by the hypothalamus to initiate this cascade?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cortisol from the adrenal cortex

explanation.summary: The HPA axis begins with hypothalamic CRH.
explanation.whyCorrect: The hypothalamus releases corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), which activates the anterior pituitary. The pituitary then secretes ACTH, which triggers cortisol synthesis in the adrenal gland.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ACTH is released by the anterior pituitary, not the hypothalamus, and acts downstream of CRH.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid made in the adrenal gland and is not part of the CRH-ACTH-cortisol cascade.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ADH regulates water balance and is not the hormone that initiates cortisol synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cortisol is the end product synthesized in the adrenal gland, not the initiating hypothalamic signal.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis is started on a corticosteroid, which markedly reduces joint inflammation. Which of the following best describes how corticosteroids decrease inflammation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They decrease production of anti-inflammatory mediators such as IL-10 and IL-4

choices.label: B
choices.text: They increase production of proinflammatory mediators such as TNF-alpha and IL-2

choices.label: C
choices.text: They inhibit both proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory mediators equally

choices.label: D
choices.text: They inhibit proinflammatory mediators and stimulate anti-inflammatory mediators

choices.label: E
choices.text: They stimulate both proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory mediators equally

explanation.summary: Cortisol shifts the balance away from inflammation on both sides.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cortisol inhibits production of proinflammatory mediators (leukotrienes, prostaglandins, IL-2, IFN-gamma, IFN-alpha, TNF-alpha) while increasing anti-inflammatory mediators (IL-10, IL-4, IL-13). This dual action reduces the overall inflammatory response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: They increase anti-inflammatory mediators rather than decreasing them.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Corticosteroids suppress, not increase, proinflammatory mediators.
whyWrongByChoice.C: They do not inhibit anti-inflammatory mediators; those are increased.
whyWrongByChoice.E: They suppress proinflammatory mediators rather than stimulating them.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A pediatrician wants a single-dose corticosteroid for an asthma exacerbation that has high glucocorticoid activity and a long duration of action so it can be dosed once and exert its effect for several days. Which of the following corticosteroids best fits this profile?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cortisone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dexamethasone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fludrocortisone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hydrocortisone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prednisone

explanation.summary: Dexamethasone has the highest glucocorticoid activity and a long duration.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dexamethasone has a relative glucocorticoid activity of 30 and a long duration of action, making it well suited for single-dose use in a pediatric asthma exacerbation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cortisone has glucocorticoid activity of 1 and a short duration of action.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fludrocortisone is used exclusively as a mineralocorticoid and has essentially no glucocorticoid activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydrocortisone has glucocorticoid activity of 1 and a short duration of action.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prednisone has moderate glucocorticoid activity (4) but only an intermediate duration.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A physician is deciding whether corticosteroids are safe in several patients. Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to corticosteroid therapy because these drugs would worsen it directly?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diabetes mellitus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glaucoma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Osteoporosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Systemic fungal infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uncontrolled hypertension

explanation.summary: Immunosuppression makes an untreated systemic fungal infection an absolute contraindication.
explanation.whyCorrect: Corticosteroids suppress the immune system, leaving the body unable to fight a systemic fungal infection, so this is an absolute contraindication to their use.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diabetes can be worsened by corticosteroids, but it is a relative caution rather than an absolute contraindication.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glaucoma can be aggravated by steroids but is not an absolute contraindication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Osteoporosis is worsened by steroids and warrants caution but is not the absolute contraindication tested here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uncontrolled hypertension warrants caution but is not an absolute contraindication.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with persistent asthma needs long-term corticosteroid therapy, and the clinician wants to minimize systemic adverse effects. Which of the following strategies best reduces the systemic effects of corticosteroids in asthma treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every-other-day dosing

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intra-articular injections

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lowest effective dose for the shortest time

choices.label: D
choices.text: Systemic (oral) corticosteroids

choices.label: E
choices.text: Using inhaled corticosteroids

explanation.summary: Inhaled delivery keeps the drug in the airways and limits systemic absorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: Inhaled corticosteroids act mainly in the lungs and are minimally absorbed systemically, so they reduce systemic adverse effects while treating airway inflammation in asthma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Every-other-day dosing can lessen adrenal suppression but does not specifically limit systemic exposure the way inhaled delivery does.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intra-articular injections treat joints and are not a route used for asthma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Using the lowest effective dose is a general principle but does not target the airways or minimize systemic absorption as directly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Systemic corticosteroids actually increase systemic exposure and adverse effects.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman on chronic high-dose oral steroids for temporal arteritis develops new-onset hyperglycemia requiring treatment. Drugs from which of the following classes are the most common cause of drug-induced diabetes mellitus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibiotics

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antihistamines

choices.label: C
choices.text: Beta-blockers

choices.label: D
choices.text: Corticosteroids

choices.label: E
choices.text: NSAIDs

explanation.summary: Corticosteroids are the leading cause of drug-induced diabetes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Corticosteroids mimic cortisol, increasing hepatic gluconeogenesis and decreasing pancreatic insulin synthesis, which can cause new or worsen existing diabetes. This makes them the most common cause of drug-induced diabetes mellitus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotics are not a leading cause of drug-induced diabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antihistamines are not a significant cause of hyperglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beta-blockers may blunt glucose recovery but are not the most common cause of drug-induced diabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NSAIDs are associated mainly with gastrointestinal adverse effects, not drug-induced diabetes.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: Cortisol circulates at roughly 100 times the concentration of aldosterone and binds the mineralocorticoid receptor with similar affinity, yet aldosterone dominates mineralocorticoid signaling in the kidney. Which of the following best explains why cortisol does not overwhelm the mineralocorticoid receptor in these tissues?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 converts cortisol to cortisone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aldosterone has a 100-fold higher affinity for the receptor than cortisol

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cortisol is entirely bound to plasma proteins and cannot enter cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cortisol is unable to bind the mineralocorticoid receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mineralocorticoid receptors are located only in the central nervous system

explanation.summary: An enzyme protects the mineralocorticoid receptor from cortisol.
explanation.whyCorrect: In mineralocorticoid target tissues, 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 converts cortisol into inactive cortisone. This 'protects' the mineralocorticoid receptor so aldosterone, rather than the far more abundant cortisol, dominates its signaling.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The two hormones have similar receptor affinity; aldosterone does not simply out-compete cortisol by affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cortisol is not fully protein-bound; free cortisol readily enters cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cortisol does bind the mineralocorticoid receptor with affinity similar to aldosterone; that is exactly the problem the enzyme solves.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mineralocorticoid receptors are present in the kidney, colon, and salivary and sweat glands, not only the CNS.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman presents in preterm labor at 30 weeks of gestation. To accelerate fetal lung maturity and reduce neonatal respiratory complications, the obstetrician administers an intramuscular corticosteroid. Which of the following is the most appropriate agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Betamethasone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cortisone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fludrocortisone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spironolactone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topical hydrocortisone

explanation.summary: Antenatal betamethasone accelerates fetal lung development.
explanation.whyCorrect: Betamethasone given intramuscularly (12 mg, two doses 24 hours apart) for preterm labor accelerates development of type I and type II pneumocytes, improving lung mechanics and surfactant production and reducing neonatal morbidity.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cortisone is a short-acting agent with low glucocorticoid potency and is not the antenatal agent used for lung maturity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid used for salt retention, not fetal lung maturation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist, not a corticosteroid used to mature fetal lungs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topical hydrocortisone treats skin conditions and would not reach the fetus systemically.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A patient is given a mineralocorticoid, which acts on the principal cells of the renal collecting duct. Which of the following best describes the net effect of aldosterone at this site?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased reabsorption of both sodium and potassium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased calcium reabsorption and phosphate excretion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased free water excretion with no change in sodium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased sodium excretion and increased potassium reabsorption

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased sodium reabsorption and increased potassium excretion

explanation.summary: Aldosterone reabsorbs sodium and wastes potassium in the collecting duct.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption by upregulating luminal sodium channels and the Na+/K+-ATPase pump. The pump drives potassium into the cell, and increased potassium channels then secrete it into the urine, so the net effect is sodium reabsorption with potassium excretion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption rather than decreasing transport of both ions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aldosterone acts on sodium and potassium handling, not calcium and phosphate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sodium reabsorption drives concurrent water reabsorption, expanding plasma volume, not free water excretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aldosterone reabsorbs sodium and excretes potassium, the opposite of this choice.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man who has taken high-dose prednisone for a year after a kidney transplant abruptly stops the medication. Over the next two days he develops fatigue, nausea, and profound hypotension. Which of the following best explains his presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adrenal insufficiency

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anaphylaxis to prednisone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iatrogenic Cushing syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Primary hyperaldosteronism

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rebound hyperglycemia

explanation.summary: Abrupt steroid withdrawal after chronic use precipitates adrenal crisis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prolonged exogenous corticosteroids suppress the HPA axis, leading to adrenal suppression and inadequate endogenous cortisol production. Sudden discontinuation unmasks adrenal insufficiency, which is why corticosteroids are tapered gradually rather than stopped abruptly.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anaphylaxis occurs on exposure to a drug, not on its discontinuation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cushing syndrome results from excess, not deficient, corticosteroid effect and would not follow abrupt withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and hypokalemia, not hypotension after steroid withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Steroids raise blood glucose while being taken; stopping them would not cause hypotension and these symptoms.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has been taking prednisone and recently added regular ibuprofen for joint pain. She now presents with epigastric pain and melena. The concurrent use of these two drugs most notably increases her risk of which of the following adverse effects?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adrenal axis suppression

choices.label: B
choices.text: Open-angle glaucoma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral candidiasis (thrush)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Osteoporotic bone loss

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peptic ulcer disease

explanation.summary: Steroids plus NSAIDs sharply raise the risk of ulcers and GI bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Corticosteroids increase gastric acid secretion and predispose to gastritis and peptic ulcer disease. This risk increases nearly four-fold when they are combined with NSAIDs, which fits this patient's epigastric pain and melena.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adrenal suppression relates to prolonged systemic steroid exposure, not to NSAID co-administration.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glaucoma is a steroid effect on the eye and is unrelated to combining steroids with NSAIDs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oral thrush is linked to inhaled corticosteroids, not to the steroid-NSAID combination.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Osteoporosis is a long-term steroid effect but is not specifically potentiated by adding an NSAID.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy using an inhaled corticosteroid daily for asthma develops white, curd-like plaques on his tongue and buccal mucosa that scrape off to reveal an erythematous base. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aphthous ulcers

choices.label: B
choices.text: Herpetic stomatitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral candidiasis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral leukoplakia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oral lichen planus

explanation.summary: Inhaled steroids predispose to oral Candida infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Inhaled corticosteroids reduce the local immune response in the mouth and throat, allowing opportunistic Candida albicans to cause oral thrush, which presents as removable white plaques. Rinsing the mouth after each inhaler use helps prevent it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aphthous ulcers are shallow painful ulcers, not white curd-like plaques.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Herpetic stomatitis produces painful vesicles and ulcers, not scrapable white plaques.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Leukoplakia forms adherent white patches that do not scrape off and is not caused by inhaled steroids in a child.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lichen planus produces lacy white striae that are fixed, not removable plaques from steroid use.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A histology student is comparing the adrenal cortex regions that produce the two most important endogenous steroids. Although aldosterone is synthesized through the same steps as cortisol, it is released from a different zone of the adrenal gland. From which of the following regions is aldosterone released?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adrenal medulla

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anterior pituitary

choices.label: C
choices.text: Zona fasciculata

choices.label: D
choices.text: Zona glomerulosa

choices.label: E
choices.text: Zona reticularis

explanation.summary: Aldosterone comes from the zona glomerulosa; cortisol from the zona fasciculata.
explanation.whyCorrect: The steps for aldosterone synthesis are the same as for cortisol, but aldosterone is released from the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal gland and has different physiologic functions as a mineralocorticoid.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The adrenal medulla is not the site of aldosterone release; aldosterone comes from the adrenal cortex.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The anterior pituitary releases ACTH, which triggers adrenal steroid synthesis; it does not release aldosterone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex is the source of cortisol, not aldosterone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The zona reticularis is not the zone identified as the source of aldosterone.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 30-year-old healthy volunteer has serum cortisol measured every 3 hours over a full day as part of a physiology study. The hypothalamus releases CRH in a pulsatile fashion, and cortisol levels vary with the time of day. At which of the following times would his cortisol level be expected to be highest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Early evening, around 6 pm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Early morning, around waking

choices.label: C
choices.text: Late night, around midnight

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mid-afternoon, around 3 pm

choices.label: E
choices.text: Middle of sleep, around 3 am

explanation.summary: Cortisol peaks in the morning to promote wakefulness.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cortisol production increases or decreases at certain times during the day, and it is highest in the morning to promote wakefulness. The brick's Figure 1 shows cortisol peaking around 6 to 9 am while awake and falling to its lowest levels during sleep.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Early evening cortisol is low and still declining toward the sleep-time nadir.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Around midnight cortisol is near its lowest level of the day.
whyWrongByChoice.D: By mid-afternoon cortisol has fallen well below its morning peak.
whyWrongByChoice.E: During sleep in the early morning hours cortisol is at or near its nadir before rising toward waking.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with adrenal insufficiency becomes hypotensive and responds poorly to infused norepinephrine until cortisol is replaced. Which of the following best explains how cortisol normally supports blood pressure in the vasculature?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It directly constricts arterioles by binding alpha-1 receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: It downregulates beta-2 receptors on vascular smooth muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: It increases catecholamine synthesis in the adrenal medulla

choices.label: D
choices.text: It stimulates renin release from the juxtaglomerular cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It upregulates the number of alpha-1 receptors on arterioles

explanation.summary: Cortisol sensitizes arterioles to catecholamines by upregulating alpha-1 receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cortisol enhances vascular reactivity to vasoactive agents such as epinephrine and norepinephrine. It maintains normal blood pressure by upregulating the number of vasoconstricting alpha-1 receptors on arterioles, which increases their sensitivity to these neurotransmitters; the resulting vasoconstriction raises blood pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cortisol does not itself bind alpha-1 receptors; it increases the number of receptors available to norepinephrine and epinephrine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The mechanism involves upregulating alpha-1 receptors, not downregulating beta-2 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cortisol's vascular action is described as enhancing sensitivity to catecholamines, not increasing their synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick attributes cortisol's blood pressure effect to vascular receptor upregulation, not to renin release.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman receiving high-dose methylprednisolone for a lupus flare develops a blood glucose of 290 mg/dL within hours of her first dose. In addition to its hepatic effects, the corticosteroid acts directly on pancreatic beta cells. Which of the following best describes that pancreatic action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beta-cell apoptosis triggered through activation of catabolic pathways

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enhanced insulin secretion that is quickly outpaced by hepatic glucose production

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased glucagon release from the neighbouring pancreatic alpha cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced expression of glucose transporters on the beta-cell plasma membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suppressed insulin gene transcription and inhibited release of insulin vesicles

explanation.summary: Cortisol binds beta-cell glucocorticoid receptors and shuts down insulin production and release.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cortisol binds to glucocorticoid receptors in pancreatic beta cells, which leads to suppression of insulin gene transcription and inhibition of the release of insulin vesicles, decreasing insulin secretion. Together with increased hepatic gluconeogenesis, this produces a dose-dependent hyperglycemic effect within hours of exposure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick describes catabolic pathway activation in muscle, not apoptosis of beta cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cortisol decreases, not enhances, insulin secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cortisol potentiates glucagon's effects in the liver, but its pancreatic action is on beta-cell insulin, not alpha-cell glucagon release.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Decreased glucose transport is a cortisol effect in adipose tissue, not the mechanism at the beta cell.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman on prednisone for 3 years for polymyalgia rheumatica sustains a vertebral compression fracture after minimal trauma, and DEXA scanning shows osteoporosis. Which of the following best describes how cortisol produces this skeletal effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increasing osteoclast activity while inhibiting intestinal calcium absorption

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increasing renal calcium reabsorption and depositing calcium in soft tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibiting vitamin D activation and lowering parathyroid hormone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stimulating osteoblasts while increasing phosphate excretion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suppressing osteoclasts while blocking osteoblast collagen synthesis

explanation.summary: Cortisol raises bone resorption through osteoclasts and reduced gut calcium uptake.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cortisol increases the activity of osteoclasts while also inhibiting the absorption of calcium in the gut, leading to increased bone resorption. Long-term this manifests as osteoporosis, fractures, and osteonecrosis, which is why patients on chronic steroids must be monitored for osteoporosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick describes reduced gut calcium absorption, not increased renal calcium reabsorption.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The stated mechanism is osteoclast activation plus reduced gut calcium absorption, not vitamin D or PTH effects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cortisol's skeletal effect is increased resorption via osteoclasts, not osteoblast stimulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cortisol increases, not suppresses, osteoclast activity.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with Cushing syndrome from long-term corticosteroid use has central fat deposits in his face, abdomen, and upper back, along with thin arms and legs. Which of the following best describes the direct action of cortisol on adipocytes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activates enzymes that break down stored triglycerides and decreases glucose transport

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocks free fatty acid release and increases glycogen storage within the fat cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Converts adipocytes into collagen-depositing fibroblasts in the subcutaneous tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibits lipolysis while potentiating epinephrine's lipolytic effects in fat

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promotes glucose uptake into fat cells and triglyceride storage in peripheral fat depots

explanation.summary: Cortisol drives lipolysis and free fatty acid release while decreasing glucose transport in fat.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cortisol binds glucocorticoid receptors within adipocytes, triggering a cascade of intracellular events that activates key enzymes responsible for breaking down triglycerides stored in fat cells, releasing fatty acids into the bloodstream for energy. It also decreases glucose transport into adipose tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cortisol increases, not blocks, free fatty acid release; increased glycogen storage is a hepatic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cortisol does not convert adipocytes to fibroblasts; it actually decreases fibroblast activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cortisol stimulates, not inhibits, lipolysis in adipose tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cortisol decreases glucose transport into fat and promotes lipolysis rather than storage.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A pharmacology student is studying how aldosterone changes the number of sodium channels and Na+/K+-ATPase pumps in renal principal cells over hours rather than seconds. Which of the following best describes the molecular nature of the mineralocorticoid receptor that accounts for this time course?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A G-protein-coupled receptor that raises intracellular cAMP

choices.label: B
choices.text: A ligand-dependent transcription factor that alters protein production

choices.label: C
choices.text: A ligand-gated ion channel that directly conducts sodium

choices.label: D
choices.text: A membrane-bound enzyme that generates second messengers

choices.label: E
choices.text: A receptor tyrosine kinase that phosphorylates transport proteins

explanation.summary: The MR is a ligand-dependent transcription factor.
explanation.whyCorrect: The aldosterone receptor, or mineralocorticoid receptor (MR), acts as a ligand-dependent transcription factor: when aldosterone binds the receptor, it acts as a transcription factor that alters cell signaling in a variety of tissues to produce proteins that regulate water and ion transport, including luminal sodium channels and the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase pump.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The MR is not a G-protein-coupled receptor and does not act through cAMP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The MR does not itself conduct ions; it increases production of the channels and pumps that do.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The MR regulates transcription rather than generating second messengers at the membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The MR is not a receptor tyrosine kinase.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A patient with primary adrenal insufficiency has abnormally high sodium losses in sweat and saliva in addition to renal sodium wasting. This finding reflects aldosterone's actions on tissues outside the kidney. Which of the following correctly lists extrarenal sites where aldosterone stimulates sodium reabsorption?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Colon, salivary glands, and sweat glands

choices.label: B
choices.text: Liver, pancreas, and skeletal muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lung alveoli, bronchial mucosa, and pleura

choices.label: D
choices.text: Skin dermis, hair follicles, and sebaceous glands

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stomach, small intestine, and gallbladder

explanation.summary: Aldosterone also acts on the colon, salivary glands, and sweat glands.
explanation.whyCorrect: While the kidney is the main target of aldosterone, the hormone also stimulates sodium reabsorption through its actions on receptors in the colon, salivary glands, and sweat glands, assisting the kidney with expansion of plasma volume.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Liver, pancreas, and muscle are targets of cortisol's metabolic effects, not sites of aldosterone-driven sodium reabsorption.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The respiratory tract is not listed among aldosterone's extrarenal sodium-reabsorbing tissues.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The skin's sweat glands are a target, but the dermis, hair follicles, and sebaceous glands are not.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The upper gastrointestinal tract and gallbladder are not the extrarenal aldosterone targets described; the colon is.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has persistent hypertension despite adequate doses of four antihypertensive medications. Laboratory studies show profound hypokalemia from urinary potassium wasting. Workup shows his adrenal glands are continuously secreting aldosterone without regulation. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his regimen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dexamethasone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fludrocortisone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydrocortisone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prednisone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spironolactone

explanation.summary: Resistant hypertension with hypokalemia from primary hyperaldosteronism responds to an aldosterone antagonist.
explanation.whyCorrect: In primary hyperaldosteronism the adrenal glands continuously secrete aldosterone without regulation, causing sustained activation of aldosterone-dependent pathways with sodium and water retention, hypertension, and profound hypokalemia from urinary potassium wasting. These patients remain hypertensive despite 3 to 4 blood pressure medications; adding an aldosterone antagonist such as spironolactone can reduce aldosterone effects and effectively lower blood pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dexamethasone is a high-potency glucocorticoid with no role in blocking aldosterone.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid and would worsen sodium retention, hypertension, and hypokalemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydrocortisone is a glucocorticoid used for cortisol deficiency, not for excess aldosterone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prednisone is a glucocorticoid and would not counteract aldosterone-driven hypertension.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome has persistent lightheadedness on standing despite increased salt and fluid intake. Her physician wants to add an agent that expands plasma volume through sodium retention without adding anti-inflammatory glucocorticoid effects. Which of the following is the most appropriate choice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Betamethasone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cortisone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fludrocortisone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Methylprednisolone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Triamcinolone

explanation.summary: Fludrocortisone is the mineralocorticoid used for POTS, cerebral salt wasting, adrenogenital disorder, and Addison disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Table 1 lists postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome among the mineralocorticoid indications, along with adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), cerebral salt wasting, and adrenogenital disorder. Fludrocortisone has a relative mineralocorticoid activity of 150 with a glucocorticoid activity of 0, so it is used exclusively as a mineralocorticoid to promote sodium and water retention.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Betamethasone has glucocorticoid activity of 30 and mineralocorticoid activity of 0, so it would not expand volume.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cortisone has equal glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity of 1 and is short-acting, not a dedicated mineralocorticoid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methylprednisolone is a glucocorticoid (activity 5) with minimal mineralocorticoid activity (0.5).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Triamcinolone is a glucocorticoid (activity 5) with only 0.5 mineralocorticoid activity.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman taking 20 mg of prednisone daily for an inflammatory disorder is switched to methylprednisolone for a formulation issue. Using standard corticosteroid equivalencies, which of the following daily doses of methylprednisolone is equivalent to her current prednisone dose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 3 mg

choices.label: B
choices.text: 16 mg

choices.label: C
choices.text: 20 mg

choices.label: D
choices.text: 25 mg

choices.label: E
choices.text: 80 mg

explanation.summary: Prednisone 5 mg is equivalent to methylprednisolone 4 mg.
explanation.whyCorrect: Table 2 lists equivalent doses: prednisone 5 mg equals methylprednisolone 4 mg (both intermediate-acting). Twenty mg of prednisone is four times the 5 mg reference dose, so the equivalent methylprednisolone dose is 4 x 4 mg = 16 mg.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 3 mg is close to the dexamethasone equivalent (0.75 mg x 4) rather than methylprednisolone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 20 mg would be the equivalent hydrocortisone dose for 5 mg of prednisone, not a methylprednisolone equivalent for 20 mg of prednisone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 25 mg corresponds to cortisone's equivalent dose for 5 mg of prednisone, not to methylprednisolone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 80 mg of methylprednisolone would be five times more potent than her current prednisone dose.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with congestive heart failure needs a systemic glucocorticoid for a severe inflammatory condition. His physician wants to choose an agent whose relative mineralocorticoid activity is zero to avoid sodium and fluid retention. Which of the following corticosteroids best meets this requirement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cortisone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dexamethasone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydrocortisone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prednisolone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Triamcinolone

explanation.summary: Dexamethasone and betamethasone have zero mineralocorticoid activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Table 2 shows dexamethasone with a glucocorticoid activity of 30, mineralocorticoid activity of 0, and a long duration of action. Betamethasone shares this profile. The other systemic glucocorticoids retain some mineralocorticoid activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cortisone has a mineralocorticoid activity of 1.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydrocortisone has a mineralocorticoid activity of 1, equal to its glucocorticoid activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prednisolone has a mineralocorticoid activity of 0.8.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Triamcinolone has a mineralocorticoid activity of 0.5.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man in the intensive care unit has severe hypotension that remains unexplained despite adequate intravenous fluid resuscitation and vasopressor therapy. Which of the following agents is most appropriate to add as a potentially life-saving measure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inhaled fluticasone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral fludrocortisone alone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spironolactone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topical hydrocortisone

explanation.summary: Refractory hypotension in the critically ill may reflect cortisol deficiency and is treated with hydrocortisone.
explanation.whyCorrect: Critically ill patients with severe unexplained hypotension despite adequate fluid and vasopressor therapy are often treated with hydrocortisone (pharmacologic cortisol). This can be life saving because these patients may have a cortisol deficiency that is causing their hypotension, since cortisol is key in maintaining blood pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inhaled corticosteroids stay mainly in the lungs and are used for asthma and COPD, not systemic hypotension.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick identifies hydrocortisone, which replaces cortisol, as the treatment; fludrocortisone alone would not replace cortisol's glucocorticoid actions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spironolactone blocks aldosterone and would lower, not raise, blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topical hydrocortisone is minimally absorbed and treats skin conditions, not shock.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with plaque psoriasis on her elbows is prescribed a mid-potency topical corticosteroid. She asks how she can make the same cream work more effectively on her thick plaques. Which of the following changes would most increase the realized potency of her medication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Applying the cream to a smaller total skin area

choices.label: B
choices.text: Covering the treated area with an occlusive bandage

choices.label: C
choices.text: Diluting the cream with a moisturizer before application

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rinsing the area with water immediately after application

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switching from a cream to an oral tablet of the same drug

explanation.summary: Occlusion increases topical corticosteroid absorption and thus realized potency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Potency of a topical corticosteroid is greatly influenced by the route and site of administration. The area being treated can increase the realized potency, an area with thinner skin requires lower potency steroids, and if an occlusive bandage is applied it will increase the absorption of the medication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Treating a smaller area does not increase absorption or potency at the site of application.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Diluting the preparation lowers the concentration and would decrease, not increase, potency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rinsing after application removes drug and reduces absorption; rinsing is a strategy for inhaled steroids to prevent thrush.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An oral tablet is a systemic route with a different profile; it does not increase topical potency on the plaques and would add systemic effects.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A pediatrician is choosing topical corticosteroid strengths for eczema in three patients: a 2-week-old neonate, a 5-year-old, and a 13-year-old. She wants to use a lower concentration in children who are at higher risk of systemic absorption. Which of the following statements about this risk is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Risk is equal across all three because topical steroids are not absorbed

choices.label: B
choices.text: Risk is highest in the 13-year-old because of larger body surface area

choices.label: C
choices.text: Risk is highest in the neonate and reaches adult levels by age 12

choices.label: D
choices.text: Risk is lowest in the neonate because the epidermis is not yet vascularized

choices.label: E
choices.text: Risk peaks at age 5 and then falls to adult levels by age 18

explanation.summary: Neonates have the greatest systemic absorption of topical steroids; the risk equals adults at 12 years.
explanation.whyCorrect: For topical corticosteroids in pediatric patients, lower concentrations should be used because the potential for significant systemic absorption is higher: children have a larger surface area to body mass ratio and, more importantly, thinner skin than adults. Neonates are at the highest risk, and the risk steadily decreases until a patient reaches 12 years old, when it becomes equivalent to adults.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Topical corticosteroids can be absorbed systemically, especially in young children with thin skin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: By 13 years the risk is equivalent to that of an adult; a larger surface area to body mass ratio applies to younger children.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neonates are at the highest, not the lowest, risk of systemic absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The risk decreases steadily from birth and equals adult risk at 12 years, not 18.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has been applying a high-potency topical corticosteroid over large areas of her body for several months for severe eczema. She presents with fatigue and hypotension, and testing confirms adrenal suppression. Her physician is surprised because she never took an oral steroid. Which of the following statements about adrenal suppression is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is prevented entirely by choosing a short-acting agent

choices.label: B
choices.text: It occurs only after at least 6 months of oral corticosteroid therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: It results from overproduction of ACTH by the anterior pituitary

choices.label: D
choices.text: The dose and duration of therapy reliably predict when it develops

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topical corticosteroids can cause it if enough is absorbed systemically

explanation.summary: Any route with enough systemic absorption, including topical, can suppress the HPA axis, and dose/duration do not reliably predict it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adrenal suppression occurs when exposure of the HPA axis to exogenous corticosteroids leads to inadequate cortisol production. Importantly, the duration and dosage of corticosteroid therapy are not reliable predictors of when patients will develop HPA suppression, and if enough systemic absorption occurs, even topical corticosteroids can cause adrenal suppression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Choosing a short-acting agent does not eliminate the risk; any sufficient systemic exposure can suppress the axis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick states that duration is not a reliable predictor, and there is no 6-month threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Adrenal suppression reflects inadequate endogenous cortisol production because exogenous steroids signal the axis to stop, not ACTH overproduction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Duration and dosage are explicitly described as unreliable predictors of HPA suppression.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man has been taking prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 weeks for a flare of inflammatory bowel disease that is now in remission. His physician plans to discontinue the drug. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Continue the current dose indefinitely to avoid adrenal suppression

choices.label: B
choices.text: Halve the dose once and then stop 24 hours later

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduce the dose by about 10 to 20 percent every few days until off

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stop the prednisone immediately since he has taken it for less than 2 months

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch to fludrocortisone at an equivalent dose and then stop

explanation.summary: Patients at immunosuppressive doses for more than 2 weeks need a gradual taper, commonly 10-20% every few days.
explanation.whyCorrect: A patient becomes immunosuppressed from steroids when using 2 mg/kg/day or more, or 20 mg/day or more of prednisone or prednisone equivalent, for more than 2 weeks. For these patients, steroids should be tapered when discontinuing to avoid adrenal suppression; one of the most common methods is to reduce the dose about 10 to 20 percent every few days, with taper length depending on the condition and total daily dose.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Continuing indefinitely exposes him to ongoing adverse effects; the goal is the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, with a taper when stopping.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A single halving followed by discontinuation is not a gradual taper and would not allow the HPA axis to recover.
whyWrongByChoice.D: At 40 mg/day for 5 weeks he exceeds the 20 mg/day for more than 2 weeks threshold, so abrupt discontinuation risks adrenal suppression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fludrocortisone is a pure mineralocorticoid and does not replace glucocorticoid activity or allow the HPA axis to recover.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman taking high-dose prednisone for 2 months after a kidney transplant asks whether she can receive the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine before traveling. Her physician advises against it. Which of the following best explains why live or live-attenuated vaccines are contraindicated in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Corticosteroids cause anaphylaxis to live vaccine components such as gelatin

choices.label: B
choices.text: She cannot mount the immune response needed for the vaccine to be effective

choices.label: C
choices.text: The live vaccine will trigger acute rejection of the transplanted kidney

choices.label: D
choices.text: The live vaccine will chemically inactivate the corticosteroid

choices.label: E
choices.text: The live vaccine will precipitate an acute adrenal crisis

explanation.summary: Immunosuppressive steroid doses blunt the response to live vaccines.
explanation.whyCorrect: Concurrent administration of live or live-attenuated vaccines is contraindicated when immunosuppressive corticosteroid dosages are used. Long-term, high-dose corticosteroids cause immunosuppression, so giving a live vaccine will be ineffective because the patient does not have the ability to mount the appropriate immune response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Corticosteroids suppress immune responses and are not described as causing vaccine anaphylaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The contraindication is about the ineffective immune response, not graft rejection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: There is no drug inactivation; the issue is the patient's suppressed immune system.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vaccination does not trigger adrenal crisis; that follows abrupt steroid withdrawal.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with a history of heart failure and prior atrial fibrillation is given a 5-day course of prednisone for a COPD exacerbation. On day 3 he develops palpitations, and an ECG shows atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. Which of the following best characterizes this adverse effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Even short-term use can induce arrhythmias in patients with cardiac disorders

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a long-term effect that requires prior development of Cushing syndrome

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is unrelated to the steroid and reflects only his underlying COPD

choices.label: D
choices.text: It occurs only after months of continuous corticosteroid therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: It results from corticosteroid-induced hypokalemia from potassium wasting

explanation.summary: Short courses of steroids can provoke hypertension, atrial fibrillation or flutter, and heart failure exacerbations in cardiac patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the adverse effects of short-term corticosteroid use, cardiovascular effects are notable: in patients with a history of cardiac disorders, even short-term corticosteroid use can induce hypertension, atrial fibrillation or flutter, or heart failure exacerbations.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cushing syndrome describes long-term effects; arrhythmias can occur with short courses without it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Short-term corticosteroid use is described as able to induce atrial fibrillation in patients with cardiac history, so the steroid is a likely cause.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick specifically lists cardiovascular effects among short-term adverse effects, not only long-term ones.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick attributes the arrhythmia risk to short-term steroid exposure in cardiac patients, not to a potassium-wasting mechanism.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with no psychiatric history is prescribed a 5-day burst of prednisone for an asthma exacerbation. On day 2 she reports feeling unusually elated and energetic, is sleeping only 3 hours per night, and is irritable with her roommate. Which of the following best describes this reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A hyperglycemic effect causing secondary agitation

choices.label: B
choices.text: A long-term effect that indicates iatrogenic Cushing syndrome

choices.label: C
choices.text: A psychiatric disturbance that can occur even with short-term use

choices.label: D
choices.text: A sign of adrenal suppression from HPA axis feedback

choices.label: E
choices.text: An allergic reaction to the prednisone formulation

explanation.summary: Short courses can cause euphoria, insomnia, irritability, and other psychiatric disturbances.
explanation.whyCorrect: While psychiatric disturbances are more common with extended courses, short-term corticosteroid use can cause or exacerbate a range of psychiatric disorders, including psychosis, agitation, insomnia, irritability, hypomania, anxiety, and mood lability. Short courses can also produce euphoria in many individuals.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hyperglycemia is a separate short-term effect and is not the described mechanism for euphoria and insomnia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cushing syndrome reflects long-term use; a 2-day exposure produces short-term effects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adrenal suppression presents with fatigue and hypotension after withdrawal, not euphoria during therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Euphoria, insomnia, and irritability are recognized psychiatric effects of steroids, not an allergic reaction.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman who has taken prednisone daily for 4 years for rheumatoid arthritis presents with fat deposits in her face and upper back, pink-purple stretch marks on her abdomen, thin skin that bruises easily, new facial hair growth, and irregular menstrual periods. Which of the following best describes this constellation of findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adrenal insufficiency from abrupt steroid withdrawal

choices.label: B
choices.text: Long-term effects of steroids (Cushing syndrome)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome) from an adrenal adenoma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Short-term corticosteroid toxicity (hyperglycemia, insomnia)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topical corticosteroid side effects (local skin atrophy)

explanation.summary: Moon face, buffalo hump, striae, easy bruising, hirsutism, and menstrual irregularity are long-term steroid effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's Figure 4 summarizes the long-term effects of steroids (Cushing syndrome): fat deposits in the face (moon face), abdomen, and upper back (buffalo hump); pink-purple striae on the abdomen, thighs, breasts, and arms with thin skin that bruises easily; and, in women only, hirsutism and irregular or absent menstrual periods.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adrenal insufficiency causes fatigue, nausea, and hypotension from too little cortisol, not features of excess.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Primary hyperaldosteronism causes resistant hypertension and hypokalemia, not moon face, striae, or hirsutism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Short-term effects include hyperglycemia, psychiatric changes, and cardiovascular events, not body fat redistribution and striae.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topical side effects are local (skin thinning, stretch marks, acne, folliculitis), and this patient has systemic features from oral therapy.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man on long-term prednisone undergoes elective hernia repair. Two weeks later the incision remains open with poor granulation tissue. Which of the following best explains the corticosteroid's contribution to his delayed wound healing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased activity of fibroblasts and mast cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess collagen cross-linking from increased proteolysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased production of IL-10, IL-4, and IL-13

choices.label: D
choices.text: Overactivation of B cells producing autoantibodies

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vasodilation of the wound bed from prostaglandin release

explanation.summary: Cortisol impairs wound healing by reducing fibroblast and mast cell activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cortisol further decreases the immune response and impairs wound healing by decreasing the activity of fibroblasts and mast cells. This is also part of why immunosuppression from long-term steroids is accompanied by an increased risk of infection and impaired wound healing.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cortisol's proteolysis is a catabolic effect on muscle; it does not increase collagen cross-linking.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased anti-inflammatory cytokines are part of cortisol's anti-inflammatory action but are not the stated mechanism of impaired wound healing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cortisol suppresses B-cell function rather than overactivating it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cortisol inhibits prostaglandin production and causes vasoconstriction, not vasodilation.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A dermatologist applies a topical corticosteroid to an area of red, inflamed eczema on a patient's forearm. Within a short time the redness noticeably blanches. Which of the following best explains this local effect in the upper dermis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Depletion of melanin pigment in the treated area of skin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct stimulation of dermal alpha-1 receptors by the steroid molecule

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased histamine release from mast cells in the upper dermis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thinning of the epidermis that conceals the underlying vessels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vasoconstriction from a reduction in local inflammatory mediators

explanation.summary: Topical steroids reduce inflammatory mediators in the upper dermis, causing vasoconstriction.
explanation.whyCorrect: By reducing the number of inflammatory mediators in the upper dermis (as with topical corticosteroids), cortisol causes vasoconstriction and reduces inflammation, along with the reduction in cytokines that reduces the allergic reaction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Skin color changes are a listed topical side effect, but melanin depletion is not the mechanism of acute blanching.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cortisol's vascular effects work through mediator reduction and receptor upregulation, not direct alpha-1 agonism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Corticosteroids decrease mast cell activity; histamine release would cause redness, not blanching.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Skin thinning is a side effect of prolonged topical use and does not explain acute blanching.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man taking dexamethasone for cerebral edema has fasting hyperglycemia. His physician explains that a major part of the effect is hepatic. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which cortisol raises hepatic glucose output?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It antagonizes glucagon and epinephrine at hepatocyte receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: It binds hepatic glucocorticoid receptors and upregulates key gluconeogenic enzymes

choices.label: C
choices.text: It blocks glycogen storage so that all glucose is released into the blood

choices.label: D
choices.text: It increases hepatic glucose uptake through insulin-independent transporters

choices.label: E
choices.text: It promotes hepatic lipogenesis that diverts substrates from glycolysis

explanation.summary: Cortisol upregulates gluconeogenic enzyme expression in the liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cortisol binds to glucocorticoid receptors located in the liver, which upregulates the expression of key gluconeogenic enzymes, increasing gluconeogenesis. It also increases glycogen storage and potentiates the effects of glucagon and epinephrine, all of which contribute to hyperglycemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cortisol potentiates, rather than antagonizes, the effects of glucagon and epinephrine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cortisol increases, not blocks, hepatic glycogen storage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cortisol increases hepatic glucose production, not uptake; it decreases glucose transport in peripheral tissues.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The hepatic mechanism described is gluconeogenic enzyme upregulation, not lipogenesis.

questions.topicName: Steroids (Corticosteroids)

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with newly diagnosed Type 2 diabetes mellitus is started on metformin. Which of the following best describes the primary mechanism by which this drug lowers his blood glucose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of glucose reabsorption in the proximal renal tubule

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased hepatic glucose production and improved peripheral insulin sensitivity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibition of alpha-glucosidase enzymes in the intestinal brush border

choices.label: D
choices.text: Slowing of gastric emptying and suppression of glucagon secretion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulation of glucose-independent insulin release from pancreatic beta cells

explanation.summary: Metformin, a biguanide, works mainly by lowering hepatic glucose output and increasing cellular sensitivity to insulin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Metformin acts primarily in the liver, skeletal muscle, and intestine. It decreases hepatic glucose production by reducing gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, decreases intestinal glucose absorption, and improves insulin sensitivity by increasing peripheral glucose uptake in skeletal muscle.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking proximal tubule glucose reabsorption is the mechanism of SGLT2 inhibitors, not metformin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-glucosidase inhibition is a separate class not covered by metformin's action.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Slowing gastric emptying and lowering glucagon describes GLP-1 receptor agonists.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metformin does not directly trigger insulin secretion; sulfonylureas cause glucose-independent insulin release.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A researcher studies how metformin increases glucose uptake in skeletal muscle. Activation of which of the following proteins is chiefly responsible for triggering translocation of GLUT-4 to the cell membrane in these cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adenylyl cyclase

choices.label: B
choices.text: AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4)

choices.label: D
choices.text: GLP-1 receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2)

explanation.summary: Metformin stimulates AMPK, the cellular energy sensor that promotes GLUT-4 translocation in muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: In skeletal muscle, metformin enhances glucose uptake and utilization by stimulating AMPK, the protein that monitors the ratio of AMP to ATP and ADP to ATP. Activated AMPK promotes GLUT-4 translocation to the cell membrane, moving glucose into muscle and fat cells in response to insulin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenylyl cyclase governs cAMP signaling and is not the protein metformin activates to move GLUT-4.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DPP-4 degrades incretins and is unrelated to metformin's AMPK-driven action.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The GLP-1 receptor mediates incretin signaling on pancreatic cells, not GLUT-4 translocation in muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: SGLT2 is the renal transporter targeted by SGLT2 inhibitors, not the mediator of muscle glucose uptake.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman with Type 2 diabetes and obesity remains above her A1c goal on metformin. Her clinician wants to add an agent that can improve glucose control and promote weight loss with low risk of hypoglycemia when not combined with insulin or sulfonylureas. Which mechanism best describes this add-on therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activating GLP-1 receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocking SGLT2 in the proximal tubule

choices.label: C
choices.text: Closing ATP-sensitive potassium channels on pancreatic beta cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Directly replacing endogenous insulin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibiting hepatic gluconeogenesis via AMPK

explanation.summary: GLP-1 receptor agonists promote weight loss and glucose-dependent insulin secretion with low intrinsic hypoglycemia risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: GLP-1 receptor agonists mimic the incretin GLP-1, binding GLP-1 receptors to increase glucose-dependent insulin secretion, decrease glucagon, slow gastric emptying, and increase satiety, which reduces food intake and promotes weight loss. Because insulin release is glucose-dependent, hypoglycemia risk is low unless combined with insulin or sulfonylureas.

whyWrongByChoice.B: SGLT2 blockade causes weight loss but does not act through incretin signaling or satiety.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Closing beta-cell KATP channels is the sulfonylurea mechanism and causes glucose-independent insulin release with weight gain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Replacing endogenous insulin describes insulin therapy, which promotes weight gain and hypoglycemia risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: AMPK-mediated inhibition of gluconeogenesis is metformin's mechanism, the drug she is already taking.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A patient with Type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease is started on a medication that lowers glucose by increasing glucosuria. Based on this mechanism, which adverse effect should the patient be counseled about?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cough and angioedema

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fluid retention and worsening heart failure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Genital mycotic infections and volume depletion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Severe hypoglycemia due to glucose-independent insulin release

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency and metallic taste

explanation.summary: By raising urinary glucose, SGLT2 inhibitors predispose to genital mycotic infections and osmotic volume depletion.
explanation.whyCorrect: SGLT2 inhibitors increase glucose in the urine, which can raise the risk of genital mycotic infections such as vulvovaginal candidiasis or candidal balanitis. The osmotic diuresis they produce also causes increased urination, volume depletion, dizziness, and dehydration.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cough and angioedema are features of ACE inhibitors and are unrelated to this mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Selected SGLT2 inhibitors reduce heart failure risk rather than causing fluid retention.
whyWrongByChoice.D: SGLT2 inhibitors act independently of insulin and carry low intrinsic hypoglycemia risk, not severe hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin B12 deficiency and metallic taste are associated with metformin, not SGLT2 inhibitors.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man on long-standing metformin develops severe congestive heart failure and acute kidney injury during a hospital admission. His clinicians are concerned about a rare but potentially fatal complication of his diabetes medication. Which mechanism best explains this complication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excessive incretin signaling triggering pancreatic autodigestion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glucose-independent insulin release depleting serum glucose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of mitochondrial electron transport

choices.label: E
choices.text: Osmotic diuresis leading to euglycemic ketoacidosis

explanation.summary: Metformin can rarely cause lactic acidosis by inhibiting mitochondrial electron transport, especially when clearance is reduced.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the intestine, metformin causes inhibition of mitochondrial electron transport, shifting cells toward anaerobic glucose metabolism and lactate production. States such as severe congestive heart failure and decreased renal function reduce lactate clearance, allowing lactate to accumulate and predisposing to lactic acidosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pancreatitis from incretin signaling is a GLP-1 receptor agonist concern, not the cause here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Metformin does not cause glucose-independent insulin release; that describes sulfonylureas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: B12 malabsorption causes anemia and neuropathy but not the acute acidosis described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Euglycemic ketoacidosis from osmotic diuresis is a rare complication of SGLT2 inhibitors, not metformin.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman has taken metformin for eight years and now presents with fatigue, a macrocytic anemia, and distal sensory neuropathy. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute pancreatitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic lactic acidosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Recurrent hypoglycemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Volume depletion from osmotic diuresis

explanation.summary: Long-term metformin can cause reversible vitamin B12 deficiency with anemia and neuropathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Long-term use of metformin is associated with reversible vitamin B12 deficiency and subsequent anemia and neuropathy because metformin interferes with absorption of vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum. The incidence is roughly 7 percent and can be mitigated with vitamin B12 supplementation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pancreatitis is a rare GLP-1 receptor agonist effect and would present with abdominal pain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lactic acidosis presents acutely and severely, not as a chronic macrocytic anemia with neuropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metformin alone carries low hypoglycemia risk and hypoglycemia does not cause macrocytic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Osmotic diuresis and volume depletion are SGLT2 inhibitor effects, not metformin effects.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A patient just started on metformin reports nausea, bloating, and loose stools that began with the medication. Which of the following is the most appropriate counseling to help minimize these gastrointestinal effects while continuing therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a sulfonylurea to counteract the symptoms

choices.label: B
choices.text: Begin vitamin B12 supplementation to resolve the diarrhea

choices.label: C
choices.text: Start at the lowest dose, take it with food, and titrate slowly

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stop metformin permanently because these effects are irreversible

choices.label: E
choices.text: Take the full dose on an empty stomach to speed absorption

explanation.summary: Metformin GI effects are usually transient and are mitigated by low starting doses, taking with food, slow titration, and extended-release forms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gastrointestinal effects are common when starting metformin but most self-resolve within one to two weeks. Starting at the lowest dose and slowly titrating every one to two weeks, taking the drug with food, reducing the dose, or switching to an extended-release formulation all help mitigate these effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adding a sulfonylurea does not address metformin GI upset and raises hypoglycemia risk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: B12 supplementation addresses long-term deficiency, not acute GI upset at initiation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The GI effects are typically transient and do not require permanent discontinuation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Taking metformin with food, not on an empty stomach, reduces GI side effects.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with Type 2 diabetes has an eGFR of 42 mL/min/1.73 m2. His clinician is deciding how to manage his metformin. Which of the following is the most appropriate action based on renal dosing recommendations in the brick?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Continue metformin, potentially at a reduced dose, since he already tolerates it

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continue the full dose without any change

choices.label: C
choices.text: Initiate metformin at maximal dose because his renal function is adequate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stop metformin immediately because it is absolutely contraindicated at this eGFR

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch him to insulin because metformin is never used in kidney disease

explanation.summary: For an eGFR of 30 to 45, metformin may continue at a reduced dose in a tolerating patient, but new initiation is not recommended.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick specifies that for an eGFR of 30 to 45 mL/min, continuing metformin at a reduced dose may be appropriate if the patient is already tolerating it, whereas initiation of metformin is not recommended in this range. Metformin is a contraindication only when eGFR falls below 30.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dose reduction, not continuation of the full dose, is advised in the 30 to 45 eGFR range.
whyWrongByChoice.C: New initiation at maximal dose is not recommended at an eGFR of 30 to 45.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metformin is contraindicated below an eGFR of 30, not at 42, so immediate discontinuation is not required.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metformin can still be used with reduced renal function above an eGFR of 30, so switching to insulin is unnecessary.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man with Type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease needs a second agent added to metformin. His clinician wants a class with proven cardiovascular benefit. Which pairing of drug and documented benefit is most consistent with current guidance in the brick?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A generic sulfonylurea with proven heart failure reduction

choices.label: B
choices.text: An alpha-glucosidase inhibitor with proven kidney protection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Basal insulin with demonstrated weight loss

choices.label: D
choices.text: Exenatide with documented reduction in genital mycotic infections

choices.label: E
choices.text: Semaglutide with demonstrated cardiovascular benefit

explanation.summary: Among GLP-1 receptor agonists, semaglutide, liraglutide, and dulaglutide have demonstrated cardiovascular benefit.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that not all agents in a class share the same outcome data, and that among GLP-1-based therapies liraglutide, semaglutide, and dulaglutide have demonstrated cardiovascular benefit, with especially strong evidence for kidney protection with semaglutide. Semaglutide is therefore an appropriate choice for cardiovascular benefit.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sulfonylureas are not described as reducing heart failure and can cause hypoglycemia and weight gain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors are not the class credited with cardiovascular or kidney protection in this brick.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Insulin promotes weight gain rather than weight loss and is not cited for cardiovascular benefit here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Exenatide is not the GLP-1 agent highlighted for outcome benefit, and reducing genital infections is an SGLT2-related concern, not a GLP-1 benefit.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman on a GLP-1 receptor agonist develops severe, persistent epigastric abdominal pain radiating to the back with vomiting. Which of the following is the most likely serious adverse effect prompting urgent evaluation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute pancreatitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lactic acidosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vulvovaginal candidiasis

explanation.summary: A rare but important adverse effect of GLP-1 receptor agonists is acute pancreatitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: GLP-1 receptor agonists most commonly cause gastrointestinal effects, but a rare and important adverse effect is acute pancreatitis. Patients should seek care for severe, persistent abdominal pain, especially if it radiates to the back or is associated with vomiting.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis is a rare SGLT2 inhibitor complication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactic acidosis is a metformin complication, not a recognized GLP-1 receptor agonist effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin B12 deficiency is a long-term metformin effect and would not cause acute severe abdominal pain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Genital mycotic infections such as candidiasis are associated with SGLT2 inhibitor-induced glucosuria.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man taking an SGLT2 inhibitor is admitted for a major surgical procedure requiring prolonged fasting. He presents with nausea, malaise, and a high anion gap metabolic acidosis with ketones, yet his blood glucose is only mildly elevated. Which of the following best explains this presentation, and what preventive step was indicated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute pancreatitis; a low-fat diet should have been advised before the procedure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis; the drug should have been held before major surgery

choices.label: C
choices.text: Genital mycotic infection; improved perineal hygiene should have been counseled

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state; the dose should have been doubled before the operation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lactic acidosis; the drug should have been taken with food during the fast

explanation.summary: SGLT2 inhibitors can rarely cause euglycemic DKA, and the drug should be held during major illness, surgery, or prolonged fasting.
explanation.whyCorrect: A rare but serious adverse effect of SGLT2 inhibitors is euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis, in which ketoacidosis develops while blood glucose is only mildly elevated. Risk is higher during prolonged fasting, acute illness, major surgery, very low-carbohydrate intake, or states of low insulin availability, so patients should hold the medication during significant illness or before major procedures per local protocols.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pancreatitis is a GLP-1 receptor agonist effect and does not cause a ketotic anion gap acidosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Genital mycotic infection is a mucosal infection, not a metabolic acidosis, and hygiene counseling would not prevent DKA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state features markedly high glucose without significant ketones, not near-normal glucose, and doubling the dose would worsen risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lactic acidosis is a metformin effect and does not produce ketosis; taking with food does not prevent this SGLT2 complication.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with Type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease with an eGFR of 28 mL/min/1.73 m2, and prior heart failure hospitalization needs glucose-lowering therapy. Guideline-directed use in the brick supports selected SGLT2 inhibitors for many such patients. Which of the following best reflects the rationale for choosing this class here?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are first-line because they carry no risk of volume depletion

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are preferred because they reliably cause weight gain and fluid retention

choices.label: C
choices.text: They mimic incretin signaling to protect the kidney

choices.label: D
choices.text: They provide slow cardiovascular protection but require normal renal function to start

choices.label: E
choices.text: They slow chronic kidney disease progression and reduce heart failure risk

explanation.summary: Selected SGLT2 inhibitors slow CKD progression and reduce heart failure risk, and guidance supports their use in many patients with Type 2 DM and CKD.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that selected agents reduce heart failure hospitalization and slow chronic kidney disease progression, and that guidance recommends SGLT2 inhibitors for many patients with Type 2 DM and CKD, including those with an eGFR at or above 20 mL/min/1.73 m2. Empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and canagliflozin have shown cardiovascular and kidney benefit, with SGLT2 inhibitors being high-yield for heart failure and CKD reduction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause volume depletion through osmotic diuresis, so they are not risk-free in that respect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: SGLT2 inhibitors promote modest weight loss and reduce heart failure risk rather than causing weight gain and fluid retention.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mimicking incretin signaling describes GLP-1 receptor agonists, not the mechanism of SGLT2 inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: SGLT2 inhibitors are recommended down to an eGFR of about 20 and do not require normal renal function to start.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with obesity is found to have impaired fasting glucose. Her clinician explains that her tissues are responding poorly to insulin. Which of the following is a recognized contributor to the insulin resistance underlying Type 2 diabetes mellitus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased cytokine release from adipocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased insulin receptor density

choices.label: C
choices.text: Leptin deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Low cortisol levels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced circulating free fatty acids

explanation.summary: Insulin resistance in Type 2 DM is driven by elevated free fatty acids, reduced insulin receptors, adipocyte cytokines, leptin deficiency, and high cortisol.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists the causes of insulin resistance as elevated free fatty acids, reduced insulin receptors, cytokines from adipocytes, leptin deficiency, and high cortisol levels.
