Leptin deficiency is therefore one of the recognized contributors. Inadequate pancreatic insulin secretion then exacerbates the condition and leads to hyperglycemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytokines released from adipocytes promote insulin resistance; decreased release would not.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reduced, not increased, insulin receptor numbers contribute to resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: High, not low, cortisol levels contribute to insulin resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Elevated, not reduced, free fatty acids drive insulin resistance.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with central obesity has a fasting glucose in the impaired range. Laboratory testing shows a fasting insulin level well above normal. Which of the following best describes the stage of Type 2 diabetes pathophysiology this patient is most likely in?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-cell failure with low glucagon secretion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autoimmune beta-cell destruction with absent insulin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Beta-cell compensation with increased insulin secretion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Beta-cell failure with overt hyperglycemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal beta-cell function with normal glucose tolerance

explanation.summary: In early Type 2 DM, beta cells compensate for insulin resistance by increasing insulin secretion, producing normal to impaired glucose tolerance before failing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Figure 1 shows that insulin resistance from adipokines, free fatty acids, and inflammation first triggers beta-cell compensation, during which insulin secretion is increased and blood glucose ranges from normal to impaired glucose tolerance. Only later does beta-cell failure occur, with decreased insulin secretion and overt hyperglycemia. A patient with impaired glucose and elevated insulin fits the compensation stage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Type 2 DM is characterized by high, not low, glucagon levels; alpha-cell failure is not part of the described progression.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Type 2 DM involves insulin resistance with progressive insufficiency of secretion, not autoimmune destruction with absent insulin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Beta-cell failure is marked by decreased insulin secretion and overt hyperglycemia, not high insulin with impaired glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: His glucose is already impaired, so he is beyond the normal-function, normal-glucose stage.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man asks what he can change to lower his risk of developing Type 2 diabetes mellitus. Which of the following is a modifiable factor that increases the risk of Type 2 DM?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic sleep deprivation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Having a parent with Type 2 DM

choices.label: C
choices.text: High-fiber diet

choices.label: D
choices.text: Low intra-abdominal fat

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regular aerobic exercise

explanation.summary: Type 2 DM risk factors include obesity (especially intra-abdominal fat), sedentary lifestyle, poor diet, smoking, alcohol, and sleep deprivation, plus genetics.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that obesity, particularly excess intra-abdominal fat, contributes to Type 2 DM along with a sedentary lifestyle, poor diet, smoking, alcohol consumption, and sleep deprivation. Sleep deprivation is a behavior the patient can change, making it a modifiable risk factor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A parent with Type 2 DM is a genetic risk factor, which is not modifiable.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A poor diet raises risk; a high-fiber diet is not described as a risk factor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Excess intra-abdominal fat raises risk; low intra-abdominal fat does not.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A sedentary lifestyle raises risk; regular exercise is the opposite of a risk factor.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman with Type 2 diabetes mellitus takes metformin and has an A1c of 6.4%, which is at her goal. She was recently diagnosed with heart failure. According to current diabetes standards, which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a sulfonylurea to further reduce her A1c

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven heart failure benefit

choices.label: C
choices.text: Continue metformin alone because her A1c is at goal

choices.label: D
choices.text: Defer additional therapy until her A1c rises above goal

choices.label: E
choices.text: Replace metformin with basal insulin

explanation.summary: GLP-1 RAs and SGLT2 inhibitors with proven benefit are recommended in heart failure, CKD, and cardiovascular disease independent of background metformin use or A1c.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that current diabetes standards emphasize using GLP-1 RAs and/or SGLT2 inhibitors with proven benefit in patients with heart failure, chronic kidney disease, established cardiovascular disease, or multiple cardiovascular risk factors, independent of background metformin use or A1c. Selected SGLT2 inhibitors reduce heart failure hospitalization, so adding one is indicated even though her A1c is controlled.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycemia and weight gain and offer no heart failure benefit; her A1c is already at goal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Outcome-based therapy is recommended regardless of A1c, so an at-goal A1c does not justify withholding an SGLT2 inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The recommendation is independent of A1c, so waiting for A1c to rise delays a proven cardiovascular benefit.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metformin does not need to be replaced, and insulin is not described as providing heart failure benefit.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A pharmacology student is describing the downstream consequences of metformin-induced GLUT-4 activation in skeletal muscle. In addition to increased glucose uptake by the cells, which of the following effects results from this activation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased glycogenesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased lipogenesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased gluconeogenesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased glycogenolysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased lactate clearance

explanation.summary: Metformin's activation of GLUT-4 in skeletal muscle leads to increased cellular glucose uptake and decreased lipogenesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In skeletal muscle cells, metformin stimulates AMPK, which activates GLUT-4 translocation to the cell membrane. The brick states that this activation of GLUT-4 by metformin leads to increased glucose uptake by the cells and decreased lipogenesis. Figure 2 also shows increased insulin-mediated glucose uptake and increased glycogenesis in skeletal muscle.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Figure 2 shows increased, not decreased, glycogenesis in skeletal muscle with metformin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metformin decreases hepatic gluconeogenesis; it does not increase it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metformin decreases glycogenolysis in the liver; increased glycogenolysis is not a consequence of GLUT-4 activation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lactate clearance is a renal and hepatic function, not a downstream effect of GLUT-4 activation in muscle.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with obesity and Type 2 diabetes mellitus has been taking metformin for one year. Beyond improved glycemic control, which of the following additional changes is most consistent with the described advantages of this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased triglyceride and LDL cholesterol levels

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elevated blood pressure from fluid retention

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased HDL cholesterol with weight gain

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased triglycerides with modest weight loss

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unchanged lipid levels and blood pressure

explanation.summary: Metformin's advantages include weight loss, decreased triglyceride and LDL cholesterol, lower blood pressure, and low hypoglycemia risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists the advantages of metformin as weight loss, decreased triglyceride and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels, lower blood pressure, and low risk of causing hypoglycemia. It also notes that metformin improves cardiovascular risk in obese patients with Type 2 DM.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Metformin lowers blood pressure; it does not cause fluid retention or raise blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metformin is associated with weight loss or weight neutrality, not weight gain, and the brick highlights LDL and triglyceride reduction rather than HDL changes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metformin decreases, not increases, triglycerides.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metformin does change lipids and blood pressure, lowering triglycerides, LDL, and blood pressure.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman with newly diagnosed Type 2 diabetes mellitus asks whether metformin will help her lose weight. Which of the following best describes the expected long-term effect of metformin on her body weight?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Progressive weight gain from increased insulin action

choices.label: B
choices.text: Small weight loss or a weight-neutral effect

choices.label: C
choices.text: Steady weight loss from urinary calorie loss

choices.label: D
choices.text: Substantial weight loss similar to GLP-1 receptor agonists

choices.label: E
choices.text: Weight gain from sodium and fluid retention

explanation.summary: Metformin is usually associated with small weight loss or weight neutrality; early loss stems partly from GI effects, and later insulin sensitivity helps maintain weight.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation explains that metformin is usually associated with small weight loss or weight neutrality. Some of the initial gastrointestinal adverse effects can cause patients to lose weight, and once these wear off the increased insulin sensitivity can help patients maintain, or have a neutral effect on, their weight. Table 2 summarizes the weight effect as weight neutral or modest weight loss.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increased insulin sensitivity helps maintain weight rather than causing progressive gain; insulin and sulfonylureas cause weight gain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Weight loss from glucose calories lost in the urine describes SGLT2 inhibitors, not metformin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GLP-1 receptor agonists promote weight loss through satiety; metformin produces only small loss or neutrality.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metformin lowers blood pressure and is not associated with fluid retention.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with prediabetes has not achieved adequate glucose control with lifestyle modification alone. His clinician considers adding a non-insulin medication that the brick describes as usable in prediabetes. To which drug class does this medication belong?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-glucosidase inhibitor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Basal insulin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Biguanide

choices.label: D
choices.text: Meglitinide

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sulfonylurea

explanation.summary: Metformin, a biguanide, is usually a first drug for Type 2 DM and can also be used in patients with prediabetes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that metformin is in the biguanide class, is usually one of, if not the, first drugs used to treat Type 2 DM, and can also be used for patients with prediabetes. Its ultimate effect is to increase cellular sensitivity to insulin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors are not the class the brick identifies for use in prediabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Insulin causes hypoglycemia and weight gain and is not the agent described for prediabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Meglitinides are insulin secretagogues with hypoglycemia risk, not the agent described for prediabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sulfonylureas are insulin secretagogues that cause hypoglycemia and weight gain; they are not described for prediabetes.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A medical student is asked to describe the endogenous hormone that GLP-1 receptor agonists mimic. Which of the following best describes the source and timing of release of this hormone?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Produced by the liver during gluconeogenesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Released from adipocytes in response to leptin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Released from the intestine after a meal

choices.label: D
choices.text: Secreted by pancreatic alpha cells during fasting

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secreted by pancreatic beta cells as glucose rises

explanation.summary: GLP-1 is an incretin hormone released from the intestine after a meal.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes GLP-1 receptor agonists as mimicking the effect of endogenous GLP-1, an incretin hormone released from the intestine after a meal. Binding of these agents to GLP-1 receptors then increases glucose-dependent insulin secretion, decreases glucagon, slows gastric emptying, and increases satiety.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The liver produces glucose via gluconeogenesis but does not produce GLP-1.
whyWrongByChoice.B: GLP-1 is an intestinal incretin, not an adipocyte hormone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alpha cells secrete glucagon, which GLP-1 signaling decreases; GLP-1 is not an alpha-cell product.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Beta cells secrete insulin; GLP-1 is released from the intestine and stimulates the beta cells.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with Type 2 diabetes mellitus has large glucose spikes after meals despite acceptable fasting values. Her clinician adds dulaglutide. Which effect of this drug most directly blunts her postprandial glucose spikes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased hepatic gluconeogenesis via AMPK

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glucose-independent insulin release from beta cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased glucagon secretion from alpha cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased urinary glucose excretion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Slowed gastric emptying

explanation.summary: GLP-1 receptor agonists slow gastric emptying, which blunts postprandial glucose spikes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the complementary effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists, the brick specifically states that slowed gastric emptying blunts postprandial glucose spikes. The class also increases glucose-dependent insulin secretion, decreases glucagon secretion from alpha cells, and increases satiety.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AMPK-mediated reduction of hepatic gluconeogenesis is metformin's mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: GLP-1 receptor agonists increase insulin in a glucose-dependent manner; glucose-independent release is the sulfonylurea mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GLP-1 receptor agonists decrease, not increase, glucagon secretion from pancreatic alpha cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased urinary glucose excretion is the mechanism of SGLT2 inhibitors.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with Type 2 diabetes mellitus takes a sulfonylurea. His clinician adds liraglutide, and two weeks later he reports several episodes of shakiness, sweating, and confusion that resolve with juice. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add basal insulin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Discontinue liraglutide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increase the liraglutide dose

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduce the sulfonylurea dose

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch liraglutide to canagliflozin

explanation.summary: When a GLP-1 receptor agonist is combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea, the dose of the insulin or sulfonylurea may need to be reduced to prevent hypoglycemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: GLP-1 receptor agonists rarely cause hypoglycemia alone, but the brick's clinical correlation explains that risk increases when they are combined with medications that lower glucose independent of glucose level, such as insulin or sulfonylureas. In those situations, the dose of the insulin or sulfonylurea may need to be reduced to prevent hypoglycemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Insulin also lowers glucose regardless of glucose level and would worsen hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Liraglutide has demonstrated cardiovascular benefit and low intrinsic hypoglycemia risk; the sulfonylurea is the agent driving hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increasing the GLP-1 receptor agonist would not address the glucose-independent insulin release from the sulfonylurea.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Switching classes is unnecessary; the combination with the sulfonylurea, not liraglutide itself, is the problem.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman started on semaglutide reports nausea and early satiety, most pronounced after dinner. Which of the following dietary counseling points is most appropriate to reduce these effects?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eat one large high-fat meal to slow drug absorption

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eat smaller meals and stop eating when full

choices.label: C
choices.text: Follow a very low-carbohydrate diet

choices.label: D
choices.text: Skip meals on the day of each injection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Take the medication with a vitamin B12 supplement

explanation.summary: GLP-1 receptor agonist GI effects are minimized by starting low, titrating gradually, eating smaller meals, stopping when full, and avoiding large high-fat meals.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists strategies to minimize GLP-1 receptor agonist gastrointestinal effects: starting at a low dose, increasing the dose gradually, eating smaller meals, stopping when full, and avoiding large high-fat meals that may worsen nausea. Smaller meals and stopping when full directly address her nausea and early satiety.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Large high-fat meals are specifically noted to worsen nausea and should be avoided.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A very low-carbohydrate diet is a risk factor for euglycemic DKA with SGLT2 inhibitors and is not a GLP-1 receptor agonist counseling point.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Skipping meals is not a described strategy and does not address the meal-related symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin B12 supplementation addresses long-term metformin deficiency, not GLP-1 receptor agonist nausea.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man has taken semaglutide for six months without difficulty. One week after his dose was increased, he reports mild nausea and reduced appetite without abdominal pain, vomiting, or fever. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute pancreatitis requiring emergency evaluation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Expected gastrointestinal effect of dose escalation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hypoglycemia from excess insulin release

choices.label: E
choices.text: Metallic taste from salivary drug secretion

explanation.summary: GLP-1 receptor agonist GI effects are most noticeable when therapy is started or when the dose is increased.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the gastrointestinal adverse effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists, including nausea and early satiety, are usually most noticeable when therapy is started or when the dose is increased. Mild nausea shortly after a dose escalation, without warning features, fits this expected pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pancreatitis presents with severe, persistent abdominal pain, often radiating to the back with vomiting, which he does not have.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Euglycemic DKA is an SGLT2 inhibitor complication, not a GLP-1 receptor agonist effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GLP-1 receptor agonists cause glucose-dependent insulin release and rarely cause hypoglycemia when used alone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metallic taste from secretion in saliva is a metformin effect.

questions.stem: In a healthy adult with normal renal function, glucose that is filtered at the glomerulus is handled in which of the following ways?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excreted unchanged in the urine without reabsorption

choices.label: B
choices.text: Largely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule through SGLT2

choices.label: C
choices.text: Metabolized within the glomerular capillary endothelium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reabsorbed in the collecting duct through GLUT-4 transporters

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reabsorbed in the loop of Henle by simple passive diffusion

explanation.summary: Under normal conditions, filtered glucose is largely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule through SGLT2 transporters.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that under normal conditions, filtered glucose is largely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule through SGLT2 transporters. SGLT2 inhibitors block this transporter so that less glucose is reabsorbed and more is excreted in the urine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Normally very little filtered glucose reaches the urine because it is reabsorbed proximally.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucose is filtered, not metabolized, at the glomerulus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GLUT-4 moves glucose into muscle and fat cells in response to insulin; it is not the renal reabsorptive transporter.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glucose reabsorption occurs in the proximal tubule via SGLT2, not in the loop of Henle.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man with long-standing Type 2 diabetes mellitus has markedly reduced endogenous insulin secretion from progressive beta-cell failure. His clinician notes that empagliflozin will still lower his serum glucose. Which of the following best explains why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It increases the number of insulin receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: It mimics incretin signaling at the pancreas

choices.label: C
choices.text: It restores beta-cell mass over time

choices.label: D
choices.text: It stimulates the remaining beta cells to release insulin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its effect does not require beta-cell insulin release

explanation.summary: SGLT2 inhibitors lower glucose through an insulin-independent mechanism that does not require pancreatic beta-cell insulin release.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that SGLT2 inhibitors lower serum glucose through an insulin-independent mechanism by blocking proximal tubule glucose reabsorption. Because their effect does not require pancreatic beta-cell insulin release, they work even when insulin secretion is severely reduced and they carry a low risk of hypoglycemia when used without insulin or insulin secretagogues.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increasing insulin sensitivity or receptor action describes metformin, not SGLT2 inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mimicking incretin signaling is the GLP-1 receptor agonist mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick does not describe SGLT2 inhibitors as restoring beta-cell mass.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stimulating beta-cell insulin release describes secretagogues and GLP-1 receptor agonists, not SGLT2 inhibitors.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman with Type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease has been taking metformin for years. Her eGFR has declined to 25 mL/min/1.73 m2. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of her glucose-lowering therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Continue metformin and avoid SGLT2 inhibitors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continue reduced-dose metformin and add an SGLT2 inhibitor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Restart metformin at a low dose without an SGLT2 inhibitor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stop metformin and avoid SGLT2 inhibitors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stop metformin and use an SGLT2 inhibitor

explanation.summary: Metformin is contraindicated below an eGFR of 30, whereas SGLT2 inhibitors are recommended for Type 2 DM with CKD down to an eGFR of 20.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that an eGFR below 30 mL/min is a contraindication to metformin therapy because lactic acidosis risk greatly increases. In contrast, ADA guidance recommends SGLT2 inhibitors for many patients with Type 2 DM and chronic kidney disease, including those with an eGFR of 20 or higher, because they slow CKD progression and reduce heart failure risk. At an eGFR of 25, metformin must stop but an SGLT2 inhibitor remains appropriate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Metformin is contraindicated at this eGFR, and SGLT2 inhibitors are recommended, not avoided, down to an eGFR of 20.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reduced-dose continuation applies to an eGFR of 30 to 45; below 30 metformin is contraindicated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Initiation of metformin is not recommended even at an eGFR of 30 to 45, and it is contraindicated below 30.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stopping metformin is correct, but SGLT2 inhibitors are still recommended at an eGFR of 20 or above.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman on a meglitinide for Type 2 diabetes mellitus has gained weight and experienced several hypoglycemic episodes. Which property of insulin secretagogues best explains these problems, in contrast to metformin, GLP-1 RAs, and SGLT2 inhibitors?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They force insulin release regardless of glucose level

choices.label: B
choices.text: They increase peripheral insulin sensitivity regardless of body weight

choices.label: C
choices.text: They increase renal glucose excretion regardless of insulin level

choices.label: D
choices.text: They inhibit glucagon secretion regardless of glucose level

choices.label: E
choices.text: They slow gastric emptying regardless of meal composition

explanation.summary: Sulfonylureas and meglitinides force insulin release regardless of glucose level, causing hypoglycemia and weight gain.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that metformin, GLP-1 RAs, and SGLT2 inhibitors have a low risk of hypoglycemia when used alone because they do not directly force insulin release regardless of glucose level. This distinguishes them from insulin and insulin secretagogues such as sulfonylureas and meglitinides, which can cause hypoglycemia and weight gain.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Increasing insulin sensitivity is metformin's mechanism and carries low hypoglycemia risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increasing renal glucose excretion is the SGLT2 inhibitor mechanism and causes modest weight loss, not gain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Decreasing glucagon secretion is a GLP-1 receptor agonist effect, not the cause of secretagogue hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Slowing gastric emptying is a GLP-1 receptor agonist effect associated with weight loss.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man restarted metformin after a lapse in therapy and now reports a persistent metallic taste in his mouth. Which of the following best explains this finding and its expected course?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Early lactic acidosis; a serum lactate level should be checked now

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypersensitivity reaction; switch promptly to an SGLT2 inhibitor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Osmotic diuresis; increase daily fluid intake and monitor weight

choices.label: D
choices.text: Secretion of the drug in saliva; it resolves with consistent use

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency; the drug should be stopped immediately

explanation.summary: Metformin is secreted in saliva and can cause a metallic taste when starting or restarting therapy, which self-resolves within a few weeks.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that metformin is secreted in the saliva and can cause a metallic taste when a patient starts or restarts therapy. This effect will self-resolve within a few weeks of consistent use, so no change in therapy is needed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lactic acidosis is a rare, serious metabolic complication; metallic taste is a benign, self-limited effect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Metallic taste is an expected, transient effect of metformin, not a hypersensitivity reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Osmotic diuresis is an SGLT2 inhibitor effect and does not cause taste changes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin B12 deficiency is a long-term effect presenting with anemia and neuropathy, not taste change, and is managed with supplementation rather than stopping the drug.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with Type 2 diabetes mellitus and progressive cirrhosis takes metformin. His eGFR is normal. His hepatologist is concerned that his liver disease raises his risk of a serious metformin complication. Which of the following best explains this concern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enhanced GLUT-4 translocation in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Impaired vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum over years

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased renal tubular clearance of metformin lowering its levels

choices.label: D
choices.text: Large amounts of lactate produced that accumulate with metformin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced intestinal glucose absorption across the enterocyte brush border

explanation.summary: Disease states such as severe heart failure or progressive liver disease produce large amounts of lactate, which can accumulate with metformin and raise lactic acidosis risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that other disease states, like severe congestive heart failure or progressive liver disease, where large amounts of lactate are produced, can have an accumulation effect with metformin and increase the risk of lactic acidosis. Metformin itself promotes lactate production in the intestine, so added lactate from liver disease compounds the risk even with normal renal function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enhanced GLUT-4 translocation is the beneficial muscle effect of metformin, not a hazard.
whyWrongByChoice.B: B12 malabsorption causes anemia and neuropathy with long-term use; it is not related to liver disease or lactic acidosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased renal clearance would lower drug levels, not raise complication risk; reduced renal function is the concern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Decreased intestinal glucose absorption is part of metformin's therapeutic mechanism, not a complication.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with Type 2 diabetes mellitus takes metformin at the maximum dose. He has stable moderate heart failure and an eGFR of 55 mL/min/1.73 m2. His clinician wants to lower his risk of lactic acidosis while continuing metformin. Which of the following adjustments is best supported by the described relationship between metformin and lactic acidosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add vitamin B12 supplementation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increase the dose to improve glycemic control

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduce the metformin dose

choices.label: D
choices.text: Switch to an immediate-release formulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Take the medication on an empty stomach

explanation.summary: Metformin-associated lactic acidosis is dose dependent, so lowering the dose lowers the risk in patients with contributing comorbidities.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the occurrence of lactic acidosis in relation to metformin use is dose dependent, meaning as dose increases, the rate of lactic acidosis increases. Because heart failure produces lactate that can accumulate with metformin, being mindful of comorbidities and reducing the dose is the adjustment supported by this relationship.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B12 supplementation addresses long-term B12 deficiency and has no effect on lactate accumulation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Increasing the dose raises lactic acidosis risk because the effect is dose dependent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Formulation changes address gastrointestinal tolerability, not lactic acidosis risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Taking metformin with food mitigates GI effects; empty-stomach dosing does not reduce lactic acidosis.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman taking dapagliflozin develops a viral gastroenteritis with vomiting and reduced oral intake. She reports dizziness on standing. Which of the following counseling points is most appropriate regarding her SGLT2 inhibitor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a loop diuretic each morning to control the orthostatic dizziness

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maintain fluid intake and use caution during poor oral intake

choices.label: C
choices.text: Replace the drug with a sulfonylurea permanently after recovery

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restrict oral fluids at home to reduce her urinary frequency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Take a double dose to offset the rise in glucose from illness

explanation.summary: SGLT2 inhibitors cause osmotic diuresis; patients should maintain adequate fluid intake and be cautious during acute illness, poor oral intake, vomiting, diarrhea, or prolonged fasting.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that SGLT2 inhibitors cause osmotic diuresis leading to increased urination, volume depletion, dizziness, or dehydration. Patients should be counseled to maintain adequate fluid intake and to be cautious during acute illness, poor oral intake, vomiting, diarrhea, or prolonged fasting, and to hold the medication and seek guidance during significant acute illness per local protocols.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A loop diuretic would compound volume depletion rather than relieve orthostatic dizziness.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Permanent replacement with a sulfonylurea is unnecessary and would introduce hypoglycemia and weight gain risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fluid restriction would worsen the dehydration that the drug already promotes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Increasing the dose would worsen osmotic diuresis and volume depletion.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man taking canagliflozin develops itching and irritation of the glans penis and is diagnosed with candidal balanitis. Which of the following is the most appropriate counseling to reduce the risk of recurrence while continuing therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Discontinue the drug permanently and switch to a different class

choices.label: B
choices.text: Practice good genital hygiene and seek early treatment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduce daily fluid intake to limit urine output

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restrict dietary carbohydrate intake to lower urinary glucose

choices.label: E
choices.text: Take the medication with food to reduce urinary glucose

explanation.summary: Genital mycotic infection risk from SGLT2 inhibitor glucosuria is reduced with good genital hygiene and early treatment of symptoms.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that glucosuria from SGLT2 inhibitors can increase the risk of genital mycotic infections such as vulvovaginal candidiasis or candidal balanitis. Patients can reduce this risk with good genital hygiene and by seeking treatment early if symptoms such as itching, irritation, discharge, or discomfort occur.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The infection is manageable with hygiene and early treatment; permanent discontinuation is not required.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reducing fluids would worsen volume depletion; hydration should be maintained.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Very low-carbohydrate intake raises euglycemic DKA risk and is not a strategy for mycotic infections.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Taking with food is a metformin GI strategy and has no bearing on genital infections.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman has taken metformin for five years. Based on the strategies to minimize adverse effects of this drug, which of the following monitoring plans is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Renal function and vitamin B12 levels when appropriate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Serum ketones and anion gap during any acute illness

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serum lipase and amylase levels at every visit

choices.label: D
choices.text: Urine glucose and genital examinations at every clinic visit

choices.label: E
choices.text: Weekly liver enzyme and bilirubin measurements

explanation.summary: Strategies to minimize metformin adverse effects include monitoring renal function and vitamin B12 when appropriate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Table 2 lists the strategies to minimize metformin adverse effects as starting low, titrating slowly, taking with food, using an extended-release formulation, and monitoring renal function and B12 when appropriate. Renal function monitoring guides dose adjustment and lactic acidosis risk, and B12 monitoring addresses the roughly 7% incidence of reversible deficiency with long-term use.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ketone concerns during illness relate to SGLT2 inhibitor euglycemic DKA, not metformin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pancreatitis surveillance relates to GLP-1 receptor agonists, and the brick recommends symptom counseling rather than routine lipase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Urine glucose and genital infection concerns pertain to SGLT2 inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Weekly liver enzyme measurement is not a described metformin monitoring strategy.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with Type 2 diabetes mellitus taking empagliflozin begins a very low-carbohydrate diet to lose weight. Two weeks later she presents with nausea, malaise, and an anion gap metabolic acidosis with ketones; her glucose is 170 mg/dL. Which of the following dietary factors most likely precipitated this complication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased dietary fat intake

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased dietary protein intake

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased dietary sodium intake

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased fluid intake

choices.label: E
choices.text: Very low-carbohydrate intake

explanation.summary: Very low-carbohydrate intake is a listed risk factor for euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis as a rare but serious SGLT2 inhibitor adverse effect in which ketoacidosis develops without extremely elevated glucose. Risk is higher during prolonged fasting, acute illness, dehydration, major surgery, very low-carbohydrate intake, or states of low insulin availability. Her new very low-carbohydrate diet is the precipitating factor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: High-fat meals are noted to worsen GLP-1 receptor agonist nausea, not to precipitate euglycemic DKA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Protein intake is not among the listed risk factors for euglycemic DKA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sodium intake is not described as a risk factor for euglycemic DKA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased fluid intake is protective against SGLT2 inhibitor volume depletion, not a DKA trigger.
